title: Reaction Time Test: When to Click and How to Read Your Results
description: Click to start, wait for green, then click again. Learn how to retry an early click, read your latest, average, and best times, and compare results.
content:
Open the Reaction Time Test and click the test area to start. When it turns green and shows “Click!”, click the same area as fast as you can. Your time for that round appears below in milliseconds. If you click before the area turns green, follow the prompt to retry. Valid results stay visible below.

Get your first result

Place your mouse pointer in the center of the test area. On a phone, tap the area directly. The entire test area acts as the start button. After you click, release and keep your eyes on the same spot. Use the large button with the prompt to run the test. You can leave the fullscreen control and results area alone during the round.

  1. Click “Click to start. When the screen turns green, click as fast as possible.” to start waiting.
  2. When you see “Waiting for green…”, hold off until the prompt changes to “Click!”.
  3. Click the test area immediately. Look for “Reaction time” in the test area and the result below.

When the test area shows “Click to try again.”, click it to start a new round. Take time to read your result before you continue. The time spent reading the result and waiting for green falls outside the measured interval. To take a break, leave the result on screen and start the next round when you return.

Where to look while waiting for green

When you start, the test area changes to its waiting color and displays “Waiting for green…”. When it turns green, the text in the center changes to “Click!”. If you have trouble telling the colors apart, watch the text. The button stays in place, so you only need to watch for the prompt to change.

The script picks a new random delay at the start of each round. Browser timers can also run late, so the previous wait gives you no reliable cue for when to click in the next round. [S2] Counting beats makes it easy to click early. Wait for green or “Click!” before you click to complete a valid round.

The prompt tells you whether a round is underway. If it says “Waiting for green…”, hold off. If it asks you to start or try again, click to begin. If you accidentally click twice and get the early-click message, release and restart when you’re ready so you don’t click too early again.

How to retry after clicking too early

If you click the test area while waiting, the prompt changes to “Too early! Wait for green and click to retry” and the status bar shows “Clicked too early — this attempt doesn't count.” The test cancels the wait, so the area will stay in the early-click state until you retry. Click the test area again, then wait for the new signal when the waiting prompt returns.

If you already completed a round, its result remains visible after an early click. Read the status bar to see what happened in the latest attempt. When the status bar shows an invalid attempt, the time below still belongs to the last valid click. Once you retry successfully, the new time replaces the old value and the stats update.

How to read the results

In a reproducible example with a controlled clock, the script turns the test area green, advances the clock by 240 milliseconds, and then clicks. The page shows “This round: 240 ms”. This example shows how to read the display. When this is the first valid result, Average and Best both show 240 ms.

FieldMeaningWhen it changes
This roundThe most recent valid time. A lower value means a shorter reaction time.When you complete a valid round
AverageThe arithmetic mean of the retained results, shown in whole millisecondsWhen a new result enters the calculation
BestThe shortest time among the retained resultsWhen the shortest time enters or leaves the set
TotalThe number of valid results currently retainedWith each valid result until the set is full

The same time appears in the center prompt, the status bar, and the results area. To log a result, use “This round” below the test area and record Average and Best alongside it. The status bar also gives a rating. Use the elapsed time for before-and-after comparisons so you can see how much it changed.

Record “Average” and the attempt count on the same line. The count tells you whether the average came from the first few attempts or from a full rolling window. “Best” tells you which time was shortest. To see whether most of your times were close together, record “This round” for each attempt.

Why the count stays at 5

The page retains up to the most recent 5 valid results. Once it reaches the limit, each new result replaces the oldest one. “Total: 5 attempts” can stay the same. To see whether the page recorded your latest result, look for the new time in the center, then see whether Average or Best changed as the window moved.

With a controlled clock, enter times of 240, 280, 320, 360, 400, and 440 ms in that order. After the 440 ms round, the page shows an average of 360 ms, a best time of 280 ms, and a total of 5 attempts. The oldest time of 240 ms drops out, so Best goes from 240 ms to 280 ms. The stats change because the set of results changes. To keep the full set, record it separately when you finish.

Use a touchscreen, mouse, or keyboard

With a mouse, keep the pointer over the test area. On a touchscreen, hold your finger over the same area. To use a keyboard, move focus to the test button and press Enter to activate it. Native HTML buttons support keyboard activation. [S3] If the “Fullscreen” button still has focus, Enter activates that control.

Keep separate records for each input method. For example, log touchscreen results from your phone separately from mouse results on your computer. To see whether a new result is faster than an earlier one, use the same device and input method and repeat the same steps. Keep your hand position and the cue you watch, color or text, as consistent as possible. This makes the original conditions easier to reproduce.

To practice with the keyboard, stay on the start screen, move focus to the test area, and press Enter. Watch for the waiting prompt. Press Enter again when you see “Click!” and look for an update in the results area to confirm the attempt counted. If focus moves to a link or another control, return it to the test button before the next round.

When to use fullscreen

The “Fullscreen” button sits above the test area. To enlarge the area, click the button before starting a round. Wait for it to change to “Exit fullscreen”, then start the round. When you’re done, click “Exit fullscreen” to return to the regular layout. Fullscreen changes how the test area is displayed. The test still measures the click after the area turns green.

The browser requires user activation for a fullscreen request and can reject it. [S5] If the layout stays the same after you click, start the test in the regular view. The page handles fullscreen request failures internally. Use the button label and layout to tell whether you’re still in the regular view.

What the timer measures

The script reads the browser clock when it changes the button state and again when it handles the click. It subtracts the first reading from the second and rounds the result to a whole millisecond. [S1] Read the result as the time between the page issuing the cue and handling the input. Timing begins when the script changes the state. The browser still needs to render the green area on screen.

Hardware refresh and browser scheduling affect when the browser can paint. [S4] The state change, screen update, and click handling occur at different stages. Whole milliseconds make the result easy to read, but the total cannot show how long each stage took. Use the result to compare attempts on the same page. The rating applies only to the time for that round.

If something interrupts you just as the area turns green, you can still click when you return and see “Click!”. The full interval since the cue counts toward your time. The page has no separate timeout or control for deleting an individual result. To compare a continuous set of attempts, mark the interruption in your own log or refresh and start a new set.

How to log results for comparison

When testing on the same device, record the date, input method, fullscreen setting, and average together. Record the attempt count and make sure it matches across sets. An average from a set that has just started covers a different number of attempts from one with a full window. If you click early, retry and record the time once you have a valid result. To start with empty results, save the old set before refreshing.

To time an activity manually from start to finish, use the stopwatch in Countdown & Stopwatch. To play a game that involves following a moving target, open Ball Tracker. When you return to the reaction time test, click after the cue appears, record valid times, and keep the test conditions consistent across comparisons.

On paper or in a spreadsheet, keep a column for the time on each round and record the test conditions alongside it. If the status bar marks an attempt invalid, leave the row blank or write “Clicked early”. The result still showing below belongs to an earlier attempt. Compare rows with matching conditions and look for any attempt that took substantially longer. Two sets can have the same best time. Recording “This round” for each attempt lets you see whether the other times cluster near that best time or vary more widely.

faqs.q: What if I click before the test area turns green?
faqs.a: When you see “Clicked too early — this attempt doesn't count.”, click the test area again to start a new wait, then follow the prompt.

faqs.q: Why does the page keep showing “Total: 5 attempts”?
faqs.a: The stats keep only the most recent 5 valid results. Each new result replaces the oldest one.

faqs.q: Will my results still be there after I refresh?
faqs.a: Refreshing clears the results on the page. Record them before refreshing if you want to keep them.
